blocks.text: The 30 letters you met in this unit are young. Turkmen has been written in four alphabets, and it changed alphabet three times in the twentieth century alone. Many Turkmen adults learned to read in one alphabet and now read the news in another.
Until the 1920s, Turkmen was written in the Arabic script, like Persian and the other written languages of Central Asia. The poet Magtymguly, in the 18th century, wrote his verse in it.

In the late 1920s, the Soviet Union moved its Turkic languages, Turkmen among them, to the Latin alphabet. Sources differ on the exact year: Encyclopaedia Britannica gives 1927, the French institute of Oriental languages, Inalco, gives 1928.

About ten years later the policy turned. By 1939 the move to the Cyrillic alphabet, the alphabet of Russian, was under way across the Soviet Turkic languages, and from 1940 Turkmen was written in Cyrillic, with a few extra letters for its own sounds. That alphabet lasted half a century.

Turkmenistan became independent in 1991, and in 1993 it adopted a new Latin alphabet. Its first version used some characters that look surprising today: the dollar sign for a capital Ş and the cent sign for a small one, the pound sign for Ž, the yen sign for Ý, and an Ñ for the ng sound.

In 1999 the alphabet was revised, and these characters gave way to the letters used today. The revised alphabet was set out as a national standard, and it is the one this course uses: 30 letters, nine vowels and 21 consonants.

The three changes left layers on Turkmen bookshelves. Old manuscripts of Magtymguly's poems are in the Arabic script; books printed between 1940 and the 1990s are in Cyrillic; Turkmen books and newspapers printed in Turkmenistan today are in the Latin letters of this course.

blocks.title: Why the marks?
blocks.text: An alphabet built on Latin letters needs extra signs for sounds that Latin never had. Turkmen chose marked letters, such as *ä*, *ň* and *ý*, so that each sound still has exactly one letter.
With the words of this unit, you can already read a first exchange in the alphabet of 1999:

lines.en: I'm Kerim. Pleased to meet you.

questions.q: Which alphabet was Turkmen written in from 1940 until the 1990s?
In the first version of the 1993 alphabet, which sign stood for a capital Ş?
questions.explain: The dollar sign; the cent sign was the small ş.
